newsitem.title: SWEDEN: INTERVIEW-Sweden studies electric export control.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Sweden studies electric export control.

text.p: The Swedish government is looking at ways to control the parts of the electricity grid used for exports, Energy Minister Anders Sundstrom said on Friday.
"The state owns the domestic grid, so it is possible that the state should also own the parts of the grid linking Sweden with other countries," Sundstrom told Reuters in an interview.
"I think it is important that the state also controls electricity exports."

Although the Nordic power market is deregulated, the Swedish state owns the domestic grid through the company Svenska Kraftnat. However power company Sydkraft AB and state-owned power group Vattenfall AB own some overseas links.
Sundstrom did not want to go so far as to claim the existing private cables.
"The existing cables can remain as they are," he said. "The state should own planned (future) cables."
The president of Vattenfall, Carl-Erik Nyquist, was surprised at the idea of locking power up inside a country through the state ruling links abroad, according to a spokesman.
Sydkraft refrained from commenting on the possible government proposal.
A parliamentary decision on grid ownership could affect the planned SwePol Link between Sweden and Poland, which authorities are considering but have not yet approved.
Svenska Kraftnat intends to hold 50 percent of the link, while Vattenfall plans to hold 49 percent and the Polish Power Grid Co one percent.
Swedish cable connections with other countries have a total capacity of 7,300 megawatt, according to Vattenfall.
Sundstrom argued that as Swedes make sacrifices such as allowing rivers to be dammed and allowing nuclear power plants, Swedish electricity should be used to benefit Sweden.
"Swedish electricity should be used to process Swedish raw materials and to give Swedes a high living standard," he said.
